reading.title: The Old Boathouse
reading.purpose: Follow a boy and his grandfather as they notice how a shoreline and a wooden dock change over time.
paras: Every October, Mateo walked down the cedar steps with his grandfather to inspect the family boathouse on Heron Bay. Over the past thirty years, the little cove had seen a gradual change, happening so slowly that visitors barely noticed it from one summer to the next. Yet Mateo could see how much the shoreline had evolved from the faded photographs hanging inside.

The water itself never sat still. Twice a day, the depth would fluctuate, rising high against the pilings and then dropping low enough for mossy stones to emerge from the mud. Constant waves began to erode the soft clay bank, wearing it away inch by inch after every autumn storm.

"Look at that corner post," Grandfather said, tapping the damp timber. "Last winter's gale made the sand shift beneath it, so the whole pier leans slightly east." Because the dock no longer felt stable, they decided to reinforce the joints before the freezing months arrived.

Rather than tearing everything down, they planned to modify the old frame by adding two angled braces that fit the sloped seabed. Mateo also helped alter the latch on the storage shed so it would close cleanly even when humid air swelled the wood.

By late afternoon, the new bolts held firm and the deck stopped creaking under their boots. Watching geese cross the gray bay, Mateo thought about the quiet transition from warm beach days to crisp fall work. Nothing on the coast stayed frozen in place, but careful repairs helped the boathouse move with the seasons.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "fluctuate" most nearly means
choices: to freeze solid during the coldest weeks of late autumn
to rise and fall instead of staying steady
to wash away all the mossy stones along the mud bank
to stay at one exact height from morning until night
qs.why: Paragraph 2 explains that the depth would fluctuate by "rising high against the pilings and then dropping low."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how Mateo and his grandfather improved the dock without rebuilding the whole structure?
choices: Every October, Mateo walked down the cedar steps with his grandfather to inspect the family boathouse on Heron Bay.
By late afternoon, the new bolts held firm and the deck stopped creaking under their boots.
Rather than tearing everything down, they planned to modify the old frame by adding two angled braces that fit the sloped seabed.
Constant waves began to erode the soft clay bank, wearing it away inch by inch after every autumn storm.
qs.why: Adding two angled braces to the existing frame shows they improved the dock instead of tearing it down.

ev.text: Rather than tearing everything down, they planned to modify the old frame by adding two angled braces that fit the sloped seabed.

qs.q: Why could Mateo tell the cove had changed even though visitors barely noticed?
choices: He compared the shoreline to old photographs inside the boathouse.
He measured the exact depth of the bay every morning in October.
His grandfather told him that the cove had been rebuilt last winter.
The visitors only came to Heron Bay after the autumn storms had ended.
qs.why: Paragraph 1 says Mateo saw how much the shoreline had evolved by looking at the faded photographs hanging inside.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this story?
choices: Old wooden docks along coastal bays should be replaced every single October.
Tidal bays are too unpredictable for families to build near the water safely.
Photographers can stop shoreline erosion by tracking storms across thirty years.
Coastlines constantly change, so steady repairs help a boathouse endure.
qs.why: Throughout the story, tides and storms change the cove, and Mateo concludes that careful repairs help the boathouse last through the seasons.

clues.text: happening so slowly that visitors barely noticed it
rising high against the pilings and then dropping low
wearing it away inch by inch
adding two angled braces that fit the sloped seabed
